structure.title: Preface and chapters 1–3 · The philosopher takes the stand
structure.text: Nietzsche asks what sort of person needs the truths a system proclaims. His scrutiny passes from philosophers' prejudices to the free spirit and the religious life. A taste for certainty begins to look like something with a history.

structure.title: Chapters 4–6 · A new measuring instrument
structure.text: Short interludes interrupt sustained discussion before Nietzsche asks how moralities develop and what divides a scholar from a philosopher. The reader who laughed with one aphorism may discover that the next takes aim at the same habit of judgment.

structure.title: Chapters 7–9 and the poem · Who gets to set the scale?
structure.text: Virtues, European peoples and nobility bring rank and value to the foreground. The concluding poem changes the sound of a book that has repeatedly asked what sort of companion could hear a new thought without domesticating it.

people.name: The free spirit
people.text: Nietzsche tests the costs of leaving familiar convictions behind. Even pride in independence can turn into a taste for being recognisably different, with its own audience and rewards.

people.name: The scholar and the philosopher
people.text: Patient investigation can equip someone to establish what others have believed. Nietzsche reserves a further, much more contentious ambition for philosophy, the power to determine what will count as valuable.

context.title: A provocation can be a trial
context.text: A passage may offer a suspicion, an exaggeration or a conjecture and move on before presenting a proof. The difference matters particularly when Nietzsche makes sweeping claims about peoples, sexes or ranks.

notice.text: Listen for changes in the membership of “we.”
notice.why: A sentence can gather an intimate circle of readers and then impose a price for belonging. The invitation itself helps show how intellectual allegiance can become a pleasure.

notice.text: Notice when a virtue receives a biography.
notice.why: An apparently timeless quality can become the outcome of discipline, fear, taste or social rank. That shift changes what sort of evidence one would need to defend the original compliment.

notice.text: Stay with the very first question about truth.
notice.why: A philosopher might expect to begin by asking which belief is true. Nietzsche stops a step earlier to ask why the person examining beliefs wants truth at all, and what value he assigns to it. The examiner, who thought he was about to take charge of the inquiry, has already become one of its subjects.

opening: A philosopher presents an argument as though reason alone has led to its conclusion. Nietzsche suspects a confession is hiding inside it: a particular temperament has found a way to make its preferences sound compulsory. He pursues that suspicion through morality, religion, scholarship, and the ideals of his own age. His attacks are brilliant, abrasive, and sometimes ugly. They make the book dangerous company for comfortable convictions, including the conviction that seeing through other people's motives puts your own beyond examination.
